claim: Human genes, especially host defense genes, have been constantly influenced by the pathogens encountered.
source: Human genes, especially host defense genes, have been constantly influenced by the pathogens encountered (Fumagalli and Sironi, 2014; Karlsson et al., 2014; Quintana-Murci and Clark, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fumagalli and Sironi, 2014; Karlsson et al., 2014; Quintana-Murci and Clark, 2013).

claim: Pathogens drive the selection of genetic variants affecting resistance or tolerance to the infection.
source: Pathogens drive the selection of genetic variants affecting resistance or tolerance to the infection, and heritable variations that increase survival to diseases with high morbidity and mortality will be naturally selected in people before reproductive age (Karlsson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Karlsson et al., 2014).

claim: Heritable variations that increase survival to diseases with high morbidity and mortality will be naturally selected in people before reproductive age.
source: Pathogens drive the selection of genetic variants affecting resistance or tolerance to the infection, and heritable variations that increase survival to diseases with high morbidity and mortality will be naturally selected in people before reproductive age (Karlsson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Karlsson et al., 2014) and draws from established evolutionary biology principles.

claim: Selection signatures vary with historical period, virulence of the pathogen, and the geographical spread.
source: These selection signatures vary with historical period, virulence of the pathogen, and the geographical spread.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of evolutionary selection.

claim: Cytokine production capacity is a key component of the host defense mechanisms.
source: Cytokine production capacity is a key component of the host defense mechanisms: it induces inflammation, activates phagocytes to eliminate the pathogens and present antigens, and controls induction of T-helper (Th) adaptive immune responses.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: Cytokine production capacity induces inflammation, activates phagocytes to eliminate the pathogens and present antigens, and controls induction of T-helper (Th) adaptive immune responses.
source: Cytokine production capacity is a key component of the host defense mechanisms: it induces inflammation, activates phagocytes to eliminate the pathogens and present antigens, and controls induction of T-helper (Th) adaptive immune responses.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: The 500FG study generated a large database of immunological, phenotypic, and multi-omics data from a cohort of 534 individuals of Western-European ancestry.
source: Within the HFGP project, the 500FG study generated a large database of immunological, phenotypic, and multi-omics data from a cohort of 534 individuals of Western-European ancestry, which has been used to integrate the impact of genetic and environmental factors on cytokine production and immune parameters.
evidence: Describes the data collection from the 500FG cohort.

claim: The 500FG study has been used to integrate the impact of genetic and environmental factors on cytokine production and immune parameters.
source: Within the HFGP project, the 500FG study generated a large database of immunological, phenotypic, and multi-omics data from a cohort of 534 individuals of Western-European ancestry, which has been used to integrate the impact of genetic and environmental factors on cytokine production and immune parameters.
evidence: Describes the purpose and use of the 500FG study data.

claim: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 534 individuals were challenged with bacterial, fungal, viral, and non-microbial stimuli.
source: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from these individuals were challenged with bacterial, fungal, viral, and non-microbial stimuli, and six cytokines (tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, and interferon (IFN)γ) were measured at 24 hr or 7 days after stimulation, generating 105 cytokine-stimulation pairs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Six cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, and IFNγ) were measured at 24 hr or 7 days after stimulation, generating 105 cytokine-stimulation pairs.
source: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from these individuals were challenged with bacterial, fungal, viral, and non-microbial stimuli, and six cytokines (tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, and interferon (IFN)γ) were measured at 24 hr or 7 days after stimulation, generating 105 cytokine-stimulation pairs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Describes the experimental measurements performed in the study.

claim: The stimulation time intervals were chosen based on extensive studies that showed that the time points used were best suited for assessing monocyte-derived and lymphocyte-derived cytokines per stimulus.
source: The stimulation time intervals were chosen based on extensive studies that showed that the time points used were best suited for assessing monocyte-derived and lymphocyte-derived cytokines per stimulus.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Li et al., 2016; Ruschen et al., 1992; Schirmer et al., 2016; Ter Horst et al., 2016; van de Veerdonk et al., 2009).

claim: Cytokine production was correlated with genetic variant data to obtain cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs).
source: We correlated cytokine production with genetic variant data to obtain cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs), which were employed to compute and compare the polygenic risk score (PRS) of the genomes of 827 individuals from different human historical eras (early upper Paleolithic, late upper Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, post-Neolithic), which were downloaded from version 37.2 of the compiled dataset containing unimputed published ancient genotypes (https://reich.hms.harvard.edu/downloadable-genotypes-present-day-and-ancient-dna-data-compiled-published-papers) and 250 modern Europeans randomly selected from the European 1000G cohort.
evidence: Describes the analytical methodology used in the study.

claim: Polygenic risk scores were computed for 827 individuals from different human historical eras (early upper Paleolithic, late upper Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, post-Neolithic) and 250 modern Europeans.
source: We correlated cytokine production with genetic variant data to obtain cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs), which were employed to compute and compare the polygenic risk score (PRS) of the genomes of 827 individuals from different human historical eras (early upper Paleolithic, late upper Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, post-Neolithic), which were downloaded from version 37.2 of the compiled dataset containing unimputed published ancient genotypes (https://reich.hms.harvard.edu/downloadable-genotypes-present-day-and-ancient-dna-data-compiled-published-papers) and 250 modern Europeans randomly selected from the European 1000G cohort.
evidence: Describes the sample composition used in the study.

claim: The individuals in the 500FG cohort present a similar genetic background (Western-European ancestry) and balanced characteristics in terms of age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and habits.
source: The individuals in this cohort present a similar genetic background (Western-European ancestry) and balanced characteristics in terms of age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and habits (Ter Horst et al., 2016), allowing us to represent the natural variability in the immune responses and minimizing the impact of the inter-individual variability in our results.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ter Horst et al., 2016).

claim: Intra-individual variation of cytokine production capacity was found to be limited.
source: Intra-individual variation of cytokine production capacity was found to be limited (Ter Horst et al., 2021,) while inter-individual variability was largely depedent on genetic variants (Bakker et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ter Horst et al., 2021).

claim: Inter-individual variability in cytokine production capacity was largely dependent on genetic variants.
source: Intra-individual variation of cytokine production capacity was found to be limited (Ter Horst et al., 2021,) while inter-individual variability was largely depedent on genetic variants (Bakker et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bakker et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016).

claim: Ambiguous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (A/T and C/G) were excluded when computing PRS to prevent errors due to strand flips.
source: In order to account for the ancient DNA (aDNA) samples being pseudo-haploid, ambiguous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (A/T and C/G) were excluded when computing PRS to prevent errors due to strand flips.
evidence: Describes a methodological decision to account for technical limitations of ancient DNA data.

claim: The estimation of cytokine production capacity based on PRS shows significant differences between populations in various historical periods.
source: The first overall observation is that the estimation of cytokine production capacity based on PRS shows significant differences between populations in various historical periods, and the strength of evolutionary pressure on cytokine responses was different before and after the Neolithic revolution.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The strength of evolutionary pressure on cytokine responses was different before and after the Neolithic revolution.
source: The first overall observation is that the estimation of cytokine production capacity based on PRS shows significant differences between populations in various historical periods, and the strength of evolutionary pressure on cytokine responses was different before and after the Neolithic revolution.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: No significant changes in cytokine production capacity were observed between individuals who lived in different historical periods before the Neolithic.
source: We did not observe significant changes in cytokine production capacity between individuals who lived in different historical periods before the Neolithic, whereas strong pressure is apparent after adoption of agriculture and animal domestication in Europe.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Strong evolutionary pressure on cytokine production capacity is apparent after adoption of agriculture and animal domestication in Europe.
source: We did not observe significant changes in cytokine production capacity between individuals who lived in different historical periods before the Neolithic, whereas strong pressure is apparent after adoption of agriculture and animal domestication in Europe.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The development of agriculture and domestication of animals in the Neolithic increased population densities.
source: The development of agriculture and domestication of animals in the Neolithic increased population densities on the one hand and the contact between humans and domesticated animals as a source of pathogens on the other hand.
evidence: Draws from established archaeological and anthropological knowledge.

claim: The development of agriculture and domestication of animals in the Neolithic increased the contact between humans and domesticated animals as a source of pathogens.
source: The development of agriculture and domestication of animals in the Neolithic increased population densities on the one hand and the contact between humans and domesticated animals as a source of pathogens on the other hand.
evidence: Draws from established archaeological and anthropological knowledge.

claim: The number of zoonoses increased dramatically after the Neolithic (examples being tuberculosis, brucellosis, Q-fever, and influenza).
source: The number of zoonoses increased dramatically (examples being tuberculosis, brucellosis, Q-fever, and influenza), which strongly increased the selective pressure and caused significant adaptations of immunity at the genetic level (Flandroy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Flandroy et al., 2018).

claim: The increase in zoonoses strongly increased the selective pressure and caused significant adaptations of immunity at the genetic level.
source: The number of zoonoses increased dramatically (examples being tuberculosis, brucellosis, Q-fever, and influenza), which strongly increased the selective pressure and caused significant adaptations of immunity at the genetic level (Flandroy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Flandroy et al., 2018).

claim: Most of the genetic adaptations to pathogens took place in the period since modern humans abandoned their hunting-gathering lifestyle and developed agriculture.
source: Most of the genetic adaptations to pathogens took place in the period since modern humans abandoned their hunting-gathering lifestyle and developed agriculture (Deschamps et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Deschamps et al., 2016).

claim: The strongest changes leading to tolerance (decreased cytokine production) were exerted in the cytokine responses to intracellular zoonotic infections (tuberculosis and Coxiella).
source: In this respect, the strongest changes leading to tolerance (decreased cytokine production) were exerted in the cytokine responses to intracellular zoonotic infections (tuberculosis and Coxiella).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Responses to the extracellular pathogens Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans indicate increased resistance, with high production of IL-22 and TNFα, respectively.
source: In contrast, responses to the extracellular pathogens Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans indicate increased resistance, with high production of IL-22 and TNFα, respectively.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The increased response to the important fungal pathogen C. albicans after the Neolithic period is validated also at the transcriptional level.
source: The increased response to the important fungal pathogen C. albicans after the Neolithic period is validated also at the transcriptional level.
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Human immune responses need to adapt to a new landscape of infectious agents depending on the geographical location and types of microbe encountered.
source: Overall, these patterns are reminiscent of the studies showing that human immune responses need to adapt to a new landscape of infectious agents depending on the geographical location and types of microbe encountered (Ferwerda et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ferwerda et al., 2007).

claim: The resistance against intracellular pathogens increased after Neolithic with higher IFNγ responses.
source: Importantly, our results also show significant patterns in changes in the production of specific cytokines during history. The resistance against intracellular pathogens increased after Neolithic with higher IFNγ responses (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1): indeed, it is known that Th1-IFNγ responses are crucial for the host defense against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria or Coxiella (Thakur et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Th1-IFNγ responses are crucial for the host defense against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria or Coxiella.
source: Importantly, our results also show significant patterns in changes in the production of specific cytokines during history. The resistance against intracellular pathogens increased after Neolithic with higher IFNγ responses (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1): indeed, it is known that Th1-IFNγ responses are crucial for the host defense against intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria or Coxiella (Thakur et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thakur et al., 2019).

claim: The resistance to the extracellular pathogens C. albicans and S. aureus is increased after the Neolithic era, with TNFα and IFNγ production increasing steadily after.
source: In addition, the resistance to the extracellular pathogens C. albicans and S. aureus is also increased after this Neolithic era, with TNFα and IFNγ production increasing steadily after.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: TNFα and IFNγ are very well known to be important for anti-Candida and anti-Staphylococcus host defense.
source: These two cytokines are very well known to be important for anti-Candida and anti-Staphylococcus host defense (MRSA Systems Immunobiology Group et al., 2018; Domínguez-Andrés et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (MRSA Systems Immunobiology Group et al., 2018; Domínguez-Andrés et al., 2017).

claim: The production of IL1β, IL6, and IL17 is seen decreasing after Neolithic.
source: On the other hand, a different pattern emerges in relation with the IL1β-IL6-IL17 axis: the production of these cytokines is seen decreasing after Neolithic (see Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: Many important viruses such as influenza and coronaviruses (SARS, MERS, and SARS-CoV-2) exert life-threatening effects through induction of cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation (also termed 'cytokine storm').
source: In this context, the decrease through time of poly I:C induction of cytokines, as a model of viral stimulation, is intriguing but potentially very important: many important viruses such as influenza and coronaviruses (severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), and SARS coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)) exert life-threatening effects through induction of cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation (also termed 'cytokine storm') (Tay et al., 2020); evolutionary processes to curtail these exaggerated responses are thus likely to be protective, and tolerance against viruses becomes a host defense mechanism (Diard and Hardt, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Tay et al., 2020).

claim: Evolutionary processes to curtail exaggerated cytokine responses to viruses are likely to be protective, and tolerance against viruses becomes a host defense mechanism.
source: In this context, the decrease through time of poly I:C induction of cytokines, as a model of viral stimulation, is intriguing but potentially very important: many important viruses such as influenza and coronaviruses (severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), and SARS coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)) exert life-threatening effects through induction of cytokine-mediated hyperinflammation (also termed 'cytokine storm') (Tay et al., 2020); evolutionary processes to curtail these exaggerated responses are thus likely to be protective, and tolerance against viruses becomes a host defense mechanism (Diard and Hardt, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Diard and Hardt, 2017) and logical inference from the data.

claim: Humans are becoming more resistant to malaria, HIV-AIDS, and chronic viral hepatitis based on PRS analysis.
source: Our results show that humans are becoming more resistant to these diseases, with the notable exception of tuberculosis, whose risk score remained stable along the period studied (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The risk score for tuberculosis remained stable along the period studied.
source: Our results show that humans are becoming more resistant to these diseases, with the notable exception of tuberculosis, whose risk score remained stable along the period studied (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a suggested decrease of susceptibility to malaria especially in the last 10,000 years.
source: The pattern of this adaptation is very interesting as well, with a suggested decrease of susceptibility to malaria especially in the last 10,000 years.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Plasmodium parasites are known to have circulated in Africa since at least the Paleogene 30 million years ago.
source: The reason for this accelerated resistance after Neolithic might be linked to a higher disease prevalence due to increased population density, as otherwise Plasmodium parasites are known to have circulated in Africa since at least the Paleogene 30 million years ago (Poinar, 2005), and we have likely inherited it from gorillas (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Poinar, 2005).

claim: Humans have likely inherited Plasmodium parasites from gorillas.
source: The reason for this accelerated resistance after Neolithic might be linked to a higher disease prevalence due to increased population density, as otherwise Plasmodium parasites are known to have circulated in Africa since at least the Paleogene 30 million years ago (Poinar, 2005), and we have likely inherited it from gorillas (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2010).

claim: A strong decrease in susceptibility to HIV was observed in the PRS analysis.
source: Intriguingly, we also observed a strong decrease in susceptibility to HIV: this is a contemporary pathogen, therefore this signal could be due to common genetic and immune pathways with other infections that were present in human populations.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The increased resistance to HIV in Europeans may be derived from selective pressures induced by other pathogens such as Yersinia pestis.
source: The increased resistance to HIV in Europeans may be derived from selective pressures induced by other pathogens such as Yersinia pestis (Duncan et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Duncan et al., 2005).

claim: The source of increased resistance to HIV is even older than the Neolithic period.
source: Our data suggest, on the other hand, that the source of this increased resistance is even older.
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is at the same time a pathogen and a symbiont, in which latent infection enhances the resistance against other pathogens.
source: This surprising finding may be explained by a concept in which Mycobacterium tuberculosis is at the same time a pathogen and a symbiont, in which latent infection enhances the resistance against other pathogens, and this is why our immune system tolerates mycobacterial presence (Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pai et al., 2016).

claim: Individuals with latent tuberculosis exhibit enhanced macrophage functions that may protect against other pathogens through the induction of trained immunity.
source: In this regard, individuals with latent tuberculosis exhibit enhanced macrophage functions that may protect against other pathogens through the induction of trained immunity (Joosten et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Joosten et al., 2018).

claim: Increased resistance against mycobacteria is not evolutionarily advantageous.
source: In this context, humanity may not be adapting to tuberculosis because increased resistance against mycobacteria is not evolutionarily advantageous.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed data and cited literature.

claim: The risk of suffering infectious diseases has steadily decreased at least for the last 50,000 years as a result of the selection of genetic variants that confer resistance to infections.
source: All in all, these results suggest that the risk of suffering infectious diseases has steadily decreased at least for the last 50,000 years as a result of the selection of genetic variants that confer resistance to infections.
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The increased prevalence of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases is associated with the immune-related alleles that have been positively selected through evolutionary processes to protect against infection.
source: It has been proposed that the increased prevalence of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases is associated with the immune-related alleles that have been positively selected through evolutionary processes to protect against infection; hence, the contrasting differences in the prevalence of autoimmune diseases between populations result from diverse selective pressures (Ramos et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ramos et al., 2015).

claim: Genetic variants associated with protection against infectious agents are behind the increased prevalence of autoimmune diseases in populations with low pathogen exposure, such as Europeans.
source: In line with this, it has been hypothesized that genetic variants associated with protection against infectious agents are behind the increased prevalence of autoimmune diseases in populations with low pathogen exposure, such as Europeans (Fumagalli et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fumagalli et al., 2011; Raj et al., 2013).

claim: A robust increase of the genetic variants related with the development of inflammatory diseases in the digestive tract was observed after the Neolithic revolution.
source: Interestingly, we observed a robust increase of the genetic variants related with the development of inflammatory diseases in the digestive tract after the Neolithic revolution (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 3.

claim: PRS scores associated with celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and inflammatory bowel disease were strongly associated with the age of the samples.
source: PRS scores associated with celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and inflammatory bowel disease were strongly associated with the age of the samples, regardless of the p-value thresholds or the missing genotype rates used for PRS calculation, showing the robustness of these results (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Variants in genes important for immune responses and involved in celiac disease pathophysiology (such as IL-12, IL-18RAP, SH2B3) are under strong positive selection.
source: Our results are in line with earlier research demonstrating that variants in genes important for immune responses and involved in celiac disease pathophysiology (such as IL-12, IL-18RAP, SH2B3) are under strong positive selection (Zhernakova et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Zhernakova et al., 2010).

claim: The PRS of traits linked with juvenile-idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis shows a decrease in genetic susceptibility with the age of the sample after the Neolithic revolution.
source: In contrast to intestinal inflammation, the PRS of traits linked with juvenile-idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis shows a decrease in genetic susceptibility with the age of the sample after the Neolithic revolution.
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: A strong decrease in susceptibility to juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis is seen after the Neolithic period.
source: A strong decrease in susceptibility to juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis is seen after the Neolithic period (see Figure 3).
evidence: Based on the PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The decrease in susceptibility to juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis is likely linked to the decreased production of the IL-1/IL-6/IL-17 axis.
source: This is likely linked to the decreased production of the IL-1/IL-6/IL-17 axis described in Figure 2, which is particularly important in the pathophysiology of these disorders (Akioka, 2019; Mei et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results and supported by citations to published literature (Akioka, 2019; Mei et al., 2011).

claim: The IL-1/IL-6/IL-17 axis is particularly important in the pathophysiology of juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis.
source: This is likely linked to the decreased production of the IL-1/IL-6/IL-17 axis described in Figure 2, which is particularly important in the pathophysiology of these disorders (Akioka, 2019; Mei et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Akioka, 2019; Mei et al., 2011).

claim: The significant changes in cytokine production and disease susceptibility in European populations after the Neolithic can be due to selective processes or important demographic changes due to migrations of human communities such as the Anatolians (in Neolithic) or the Yamnaya populations from the Pontic steppe (during the Bronze Age).
source: The significant changes in cytokine production and disease susceptibility in European populations after the Neolithic can be due to selective processes on the one hand (as described above), but also due to important demographic changes due to migrations of human communities such as the Anatolians (in Neolithic) or the Yamnaya populations from the Pontic steppe (during the Bronze Age) (Racimo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Racimo et al., 2020).

claim: Several loci associated with inflammatory diseases displayed a group of alleles linked with Crohn's disease, celiac disease, and ulcerative colitis in Neolithic Aegeans, the community that spread farming across Europe.
source: In this regard, several loci associated with inflammatory diseases displayed a group of alleles linked with Crohn's disease, celiac disease, and ulcerative colitis in Neolithic Aegeans, the community that spread farming across Europe (Hofmanová et al., 2016), with several of these alleles showing signs of positive selection in modern Europeans (Raj et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hofmanová et al., 2016; Raj et al., 2013).

claim: Several alleles linked with Crohn's disease, celiac disease, and ulcerative colitis show signs of positive selection in modern Europeans.
source: In this regard, several loci associated with inflammatory diseases displayed a group of alleles linked with Crohn's disease, celiac disease, and ulcerative colitis in Neolithic Aegeans, the community that spread farming across Europe (Hofmanová et al., 2016), with several of these alleles showing signs of positive selection in modern Europeans (Raj et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Raj et al., 2013).

claim: The gene expression PRS of TNFα based on the cis- and trans-eQTLs displayed a very strong association with time after the Neolithic revolution.
source: In addition, the gene expression PRS of several cytokines based on the cis- and trans- [gene] expression quantitative trait locus (eQTLs) from the eQTLGen Consortium (https://www.eqtlgen.org/) displayed a very strong association with time for TNFα after the Neolithic revolution (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on the gene expression PRS analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The advent of the Neolithic lifestyle was a milestone for human societies.
source: The advent of the Neolithic lifestyle was a milestone for human societies: after the Neolithic, the density of human populations and the rate of contact with domesticated animals increased significantly, which increased the emergence of pathogens and the ease with which those could spread.
evidence: Draws from established archaeological and anthropological knowledge.

claim: After the Neolithic, the density of human populations and the rate of contact with domesticated animals increased significantly, which increased the emergence of pathogens and the ease with which those could spread.
source: The advent of the Neolithic lifestyle was a milestone for human societies: after the Neolithic, the density of human populations and the rate of contact with domesticated animals increased significantly, which increased the emergence of pathogens and the ease with which those could spread.
evidence: Draws from established archaeological and anthropological knowledge.

claim: While various events and conditions throughout human history have influenced our immune responses to pathogens, the advent of the Neolithic lifestyle was an important turning point for our capacity to respond to pathogens.
source: Our data show that while various events and conditions throughout human history have influenced our immune responses to pathogens, the advent of the Neolithic lifestyle was an important turning point for our capacity to respond to pathogens.
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The advent of the Neolithic era was a turning point for the evolution of immune-mediated traits in European populations, driving the expansion of alleles that favor the development of tolerance against intracellular pathogens and promote inflammatory responses against extracellular microbes.
source: Collectively, our results show that the advent of the Neolithic era was a turning point for the evolution of immune-mediated traits in European populations, driving the expansion of alleles that favor the development of tolerance against intracellular pathogens and promote inflammatory responses against extracellular microbes.
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The evolution of immune-mediated traits after the Neolithic is associated with a higher presence of genetic traits related with inflammatory and auto-immune diseases of the digestive tract and a lower number of alleles linked with the development of arthritis.
source: This is associated with a higher presence of genetic traits related with inflammatory and auto-immune diseases of the digestive tract and a lower number of alleles linked with the development of arthritis.
evidence: Based on inference from the PRS analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The results are obtained using European aDNA samples and GWAS summary statistics computed using European cohorts.
source: It is important to underline that our results are obtained using European aDNA samples and GWAS summary statistics computed using European cohorts.
evidence: Describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The results would be specific to European populations and should be interpreted with caution for populations from other geographical locations.
source: Therefore, our results would be specific to European populations and should be interpreted with caution for populations from other geographical locations.
evidence: Logical inference from the study design and data sources.

claim: Ancient DNA genotype data were downloaded from version 37.2 of the published aDNA genotype database, compiled by and available on the David Reich Lab website.
source: Ancient DNA genotype data were downloaded from version 37.2 of the published aDNA genotype database, compiled by and available on the David Reich Lab website (https://reich.hms.harvard.edu/downloadable-genotypes-present-day-and-ancient-dna-data-compiled-published-papers).
evidence: Describes the data source used in the study.

claim: The aDNA samples consisted of pseudo-haploid genotype data due to the low genotyping coverage.
source: The aDNA samples consisted of pseudo-haploid genotype data. This was due to the low genotyping coverage.
evidence: Describes the technical characteristics of the ancient DNA data.

claim: Samples with variant missingness above 96% were filtered out using Plink.
source: Samples with variant missingness above 96% were filtered out using Plink (Purcell et al., 2007).
evidence: Describes the data filtering methodology used in the study.

claim: Only samples within Europe were used for this study, selected based on their geographic location (latitude within 35 and 70 degrees north and longitude within 10 degrees west and 40 degrees east).
source: Only samples within Europe were used for this study, and these samples were selected based on their geographic location, that is latitude (within 35 and 70 degrees north) and longitude (within 10 degrees west and 40 degrees east).
evidence: Describes the sample selection criteria used in the study.

claim: The dataset resulted in 827 ancient samples and 250 modern samples containing 1,233,013 variants.
source: This resulted in a dataset of 827 ancient samples and 250 modern samples containing 1,233,013 variants.
evidence: Describes the final dataset composition used in the study.

claim: Summary statistics for complex traits were obtained from the UK Biobank and the GWAS catalog last accessed on March 29, 2020.
source: Summary statistics for complex traits were obtained from the UK Biobank (Bycroft et al., 2018) and the GWAS catalog (MacArthur et al., 2017) last accessed on March 29, 2020.
evidence: Describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The stimulated cytokine response summary statistics from the 500FG cohort of the HFGP were used.
source: The stimulated cytokine response summary statistics from the 500FG cohort of the HFGP were used (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes the data source used in the study.

claim: The trajectories observed in the results are consistent regardless of the sample size.
source: This analysis showed that the trajectories observed in our results are consistent regardless of the sample size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on the down-sampling analysis results presented in the study and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
